Truck-based logistics in Pakistan often depends on fragmented coordination among customers, drivers and administrators through calls, messages and paper records. Captain Truck is a comprehensive real-time logistics and dispatch platform that connects a Flutter Customer Android app, a Flutter Driver Android app and a React Admin dashboard to a NestJS API and PostgreSQL database. The platform supports OpenStreetMap-based route comparison, on-device AI-assisted fare estimation with customer proposals within an

administrator-configured band, admin-mediated driver willingness and assignment, Socket.IO GPS tracking with offline-aware driver maps, in-app chat with media upload, FCM notifications, Cash-on-Pickup and Stripe Test Mode payments, and an auditable commission ledger. Built on free-tier infrastructure suitable for an FYP, Captain Truck aims to deliver a controlled end-to-end dispatch workflow from booking through trip completion and financial reconciliation.

Road freight in Pakistan is large but highly fragmented: most operators own only a few trucks, and shippers still depend on informal brokers for load matching, pricing and cash settlement. Customers lack a single place to request a truck, compare routes, see a clear trip cost and track the vehicle live. Drivers lack a reliable assignment and navigation workflow. Administrators have no central panel for approve/reject decisions, driver–truck assignment, live GPS oversight, chat moderation, cash confirmation

is a comprehensive real-time logistics and dispatch platform with four surfaces: a Flutter Customer app (Android), a Flutter Driver app (Android), a React Admin web panel (Vite + Tailwind, hosted on Vercel), and a shared NestJS API (TypeScript) on an Oracle Cloud Always Free VM. Customers create dispatch requests with pickup/drop, truck type and count; the server offers 2–3 OSM route options with on-device AI trip-cost estimates; an administrator reviews, approves or rejects, and assigns a driver and truck

; the trip is tracked over Socket.IO GPS; customer and driver chat (text, image, voice) with Smart Reply on mobile and 90-day auto-delete; payment is Cash-on-Pickup or Stripe Test Mode; and a commission ledger records what each driver owes the platform.

Data lives in PostgreSQL (Neon free tier), with Redis for live location and locks, Cloudinary for media, FCM for push, and OpenStreetMap services (Nominatim, Photon, OSRM) for maps and routing — all chosen to keep FYP cash spend near zero.

This chapter assesses whether the project is feasible, fixes its scope, estimates its cost and schedule, and introduces the team, tools, vision, risks and product features. Development follows the Waterfall Model: work proceeds in sequential phases — planning and proposal, requirements, system design, implementation (front-end, database, then core modules and AI), integration, testing and debugging, optimization, and final product delivery — with university milestones (proposal defense, progress report, Del
iverable 1, internal defense) placed on that linear plan.

When an organization or individual initiates a new project, one of the first steps is to determine its feasibility — whether the idea is practical, achievable, and worth pursuing. Following the supervisor’s sample feasibility-study format, each area below states an Assessment and Findings. Captain Truck was assessed for technical, operational, economic, schedule, specification, information, motivational, and legal and ethical feasibility.
There are many types of feasibilities:

The technical feasibility study evaluates whether the team has the necessary skills and resources to develop Captain Truck. The project will use Flutter (Dart) for the Customer and Driver Android apps, React with Vite and Tailwind for the Admin dashboard, NestJS with TypeScript for the backend API, PostgreSQL (Neon) with Prisma for persistence, Socket.IO for realtime GPS and chat, Redis for live location/coordination, OpenStreetMap services (Nominatim, Photon, OSRM) for maps and routing, Cloudinary for medi

a, FCM for push, and Cash-on-Pickup plus Stripe Test Mode for payments. On-device TFLite trip-cost estimation and ML Kit Smart Reply avoid a paid cloud generative-AI dependency. The API is hosted on an Oracle Cloud Always Free VM.

The development team is proficient in NestJS/TypeScript, React and Flutter fundamentals from coursework and prior practice, and the locked stack matches those skills. Gaps remain around production hardening of public OSRM/Nominatim rate limits, free-tier Neon sleep behaviour, offline map tile licensing, and TFLite model training/evaluation as a process separate from on-device inference. To address these gaps, the team will use documented timeouts and graceful fallbacks for OSM, connection pooling for Neon,

a tile provider whose terms permit intended caching, supervisor reviews of AI evaluation limits, and free-tier Stripe Test Mode only (no live production payment claim). Overall, the required technologies are available and the residual skill/risk gaps are manageable within an FYP.
Free tier; in-memory fallback for demos
Test keys free; no live charges

This feasibility study examines how Captain Truck will fit into existing shipper, driver and admin workflows and whether users will be able to adapt to the new system. Today, booking and dispatch are often handled through calls, messaging apps and paper notes. The new platform provides a Customer app for requests, routes, fare proposals and tracking; a Driver app for willingness, assignment, status, GPS and cash confirmation; and a browser Admin dashboard for approvals, assignment and reconciliation.

The system is expected to streamline dispatch coordination, route/fare agreement, live tracking and commission reconciliation. However, some users are accustomed to informal broker/WhatsApp habits and may resist moving approvals and cash confirmation into the app. To facilitate adoption, the team keeps admin-mediated assignment (no automatic matching), plans demo-oriented training/walkthroughs for the three roles, and gathers supervisor and peer feedback during development so usability concerns can be incor

The economic feasibility analysis focuses on the cost of developing Captain Truck versus the expected benefits. This includes estimated development effort/cost at market rates, ongoing free-tier cloud maintenance, and productivity/transparency gains from digitised dispatch.

Function Point Analysis (Section 1.4.1) values development effort at 26.09 person-months, or PKR 2,348,190 at a junior market labour rate. For an FYP this labour is contributed by the student team, so cash spend is limited to a Google Play developer account, internet, electricity and printing, while Neon, Redis/Upstash, Cloudinary, Vercel, Oracle Always Free, FCM and Stripe Test Mode stay on free tiers. Benefits include clearer route/cost options, admin-mediated assignment quality, dual cash/online payment

records, and less lost commission reconciliation — plus intangible skill gains for the team. Given near-zero cash outlay against these benefits, the project is economically feasible within the FYP budget.

The schedule feasibility study evaluates whether Captain Truck can be completed within the academic timeframe. The planned calendar runs from 3 September 2026 to 16 April 2027 (226 days on the Waterfall Gantt in Section 1.7), covering planning, proposal, requirements, design, implementation, integration, testing, optimization and final delivery, with university milestones on the same linear plan.

The timeline is demanding because of multi-client surfaces (two Flutter apps, Admin, NestJS API), OSM routing, AI fare proposal, willingness/assignment, offline maps, chat/media, and dual payment/ledger behaviour. To manage this, the team follows the instructor-required Waterfall sequence with gated phases rather than open-ended feature growth, places proposal defense, progress report, Deliverable 1 and internal defense on the Gantt, and keeps exclusions explicit (no live Stripe production claim, no auto-ma

tching, no bilty suite). The CPM critical path (Section 1.6) shows that delaying critical activities delays final delivery, so milestone buffers and weekly supervisor checkpoints are used to keep the plan achievable.
Specification feasibility checks whether requirements are clear, complete enough to build, and bounded so the team is not pulled into unbounded scope.

Behaviour is fixed by the updated FYP proposal (15 modules), the locked product stack, and backend/admin phase plans. CHAPTER 2: SOFTWARE REQUIREMENT SPECIFICATION (FOR OBJECT ORIENTED APPROACH)

A Software Requirements Specification (SRS) for an object-oriented project like Captain Truck covers functional, non-functional, and interface requirements. This chapter captures, structures, and represents stakeholder needs so they can be correctly embodied in the system. The OO SRS activities used here follow the same outline as the NeoTeach sample SRS:
Captain Truck is specified as four cooperating surfaces that share one NestJS API:
React Admin web panel (Vite + Tailwind → Vercel)
NestJS API + Socket.IO realtime (Oracle Always Free VM) with PostgreSQL (Neon)

Core behaviours required by the updated proposal: JWT role-based auth; truck types and versioned base rates; dispatch lifecycle; up to three OSM routes; on-device AI trip cost with customer fare proposal inside an admin-configured band; admin approve/reject; driver willingness then assignment; trip lifecycle with Socket.IO GPS and offline map caching; chat (text/image/voice) with Smart Reply on mobile and 90-day TTL; Cash-on-Pickup and Stripe Test Mode with distinct reconciliation; commission ledger; FCM push; Admin operational dashboard.

The following clauses describe the system specifications for Captain Truck (NeoTeach-style clauses).

Captain Truck is a real-time logistics and dispatch platform that digitises admin-mediated full-truckload booking for shippers and drivers in Pakistan. Customers create dispatch requests with pickup/drop, truck type and count; the platform returns OSM route alternatives; an on-device AI model estimates trip cost; the customer proposes a fare within an administrator-configured adjustment band; an administrator reviews, rejects with reason, confirms driver willingness, and assigns a driver and truck; the trip is tracked live (with offline map support for drivers); participants chat; payment is cash-on-pickup or Stripe Test Mode; and a commission ledger records platform commission and method-specific payables/remittances.

Road freight in Pakistan is fragmented. Small operators and shippers often rely on informal brokers for matching, pricing and cash settlement. Gaps include opaque trip cost, weak live tracking, informal assignment, unclear driver willingness, and poor commission reconciliation across cash versus online collection. Digital load boards improve discovery but often omit a human admin assignment loop, customer-adjustable AI pricing, dual cash/card settlement with separate accounting directions, and a full ops panel. Captain Truck fills that gap with OSM multi-route choice, TFLite AI trip cost (on device), customer fare proposal, Socket.IO GPS, offline-aware driver maps, chat with retention policy, Cash + Stripe Test Mode, and an auditable commission ledger on free-tier infrastructure.
Captain Truck is developed by students of the Department of Software Engineering, University of Gujrat, under Mr. Touqeer Ul Ameen.
Flutter Customer & Driver apps; maps & on-device AI

The team applies NestJS, Flutter, React, PostgreSQL (Prisma/Neon), Redis (optional/coordination), Socket.IO, Cloudinary, FCM and Stripe Test Mode. Development follows the Waterfall Model (Chapter 1): planning → requirements → design → implementation → integration → testing → optimization → delivery (September 2026 – June 2027), with university milestones placed on that linear plan.

Informal WhatsApp/broker workflows remain common. Commercial logistics apps and load boards exist but may be costly, closed, region-limited, or mismatched to FYP constraints (free tiers, Android-first, admin mediation, no automatic matching). Captain Truck targets an academic, free-tier, admin-mediated MVP that is still mobile-ready via versioned REST (/api/v1) and Socket.IO (/realtime). Named commercial comparisons in the proposal must be verified against current public documentation before final submission.
Captain Truck focuses on three regions of capability:
Customer booking and pricing — request creation, route comparison, AI estimate, fare proposal within band, status visibility, payment choice, live track and chat.
Driver trip fulfilment — receive willingness inquiry and assignment, navigate with cached maps, publish GPS, update trip status, chat, confirm cash collection.

Admin operations and reconciliation — user/driver management, truck types and rate history, pending queue, approve/reject, willingness, assign, live ops map, payments oversight, commission ledger and adjustments.

Current practice for many small shippers and operators depends on phone calls, messaging apps, paper notes and separate tracking tools. Route comparison and fare agreement are informal. Driver assignment is verbal. Live location may be shared ad hoc. Cash collected on the road is hard to reconcile with platform commission. Online test/demo payment flows are rarely integrated with the same dispatch record.

These existing approaches cover basic communication but fail to provide a single controlled workflow for routes, AI-informed but customer-adjustable fare, mandatory admin review, driver willingness, offline-aware maps, dual payment accounting and an auditable ledger. Captain Truck addresses that gap within the exclusions listed in the updated proposal (no bilty suite, no auto-matching, no live Stripe production claim, no IoT/NADRA).

Shall statements are grouped by the 15 updated-proposal modules. Wording matches the proposal and is refined where Chapter 1 / API behaviour is already locked (integer cents, JWT roles, Socket.IO rooms, Cloudinary signed uploads, Waterfall process).
The system shall allow a customer to create an account with email, phone (optional), full name and password, storing a hashed password and assigning role CUSTOMER server-side.
The system shall authenticate customer, driver and admin users with email/password and issue a short-lived JWT access token plus a rotatable refresh token.
The system shall allow authenticated users to refresh sessions and logout by revoking refresh tokens; refresh-token reuse shall revoke the token family.
The system shall expose a current-user endpoint (GET /auth/me) so a client can retrieve the authenticated user profile and role.
The system shall allow only an admin to create driver accounts; public self-registration as driver or admin shall be impossible.
The system shall apply role-based access control for Customer, Driver and Admin on protected REST and Socket.IO actions.
The system shall apply temporary lockout or rate limiting after repeated failed logins; passwords and secrets shall not be stored in plaintext.
The system shall prevent login for disabled (and where applicable pending/rejected) accounts.
The system shall allow a user to view and update only permitted profile fields for their own account.
The system shall support driver profiles including licence details and availability information.
The system shall allow an admin to search and filter users and drivers, enable or disable accounts, edit administrative profile fields, and create driver accounts.

The system shall ensure disabled accounts cannot start new authenticated sessions or perform protected actions; the last active admin shall not be disabled; a driver with active trips shall not be disabled.
The system shall allow an admin to create, update and deactivate truck categories.
The system shall version base-rate changes with an effective date / history.
The system shall copy the applicable rate version into a dispatch request at create time so later rate changes do not silently alter an existing proposal (lockedBaseRateCents).
The system shall expose active truck types and current rates to customers; example rates are configurable demonstration data, not fixed market prices.
The system shall reject zero or negative rates.
The system shall allow a customer to enter truck count, truck type, pickup and drop-off addresses, optional map pins, desired pickup date, and notes when creating a request.
The system shall enforce a controlled lifecycle including Draft (if implemented), Awaiting Route Selection, Pending Admin, Approved or Rejected, and Assigned once a driver/truck is confirmed.
The system shall permit cancellation only in defined pre-trip states.
The system shall create a trip record only after the request has been approved and assigned.

The system shall reject past pickup times, identical pickup/drop, invalid coordinates, unauthenticated create, and over-limit truck counts; customers shall list/view only their own requests (admin may view any).
The system shall use geocoding/autocomplete services such as Nominatim and Photon and request route alternatives from OSRM.

The system shall display up to three alternatives with distance, estimated duration and route geometry when available; the fastest route may be labelled Recommended while the customer remains able to select another available route.
The system shall, if only one route is returned or routing fails, display the available result or a clear retry/fallback message without crashing the API process.
The system shall require public OSM service usage to follow the respective providers’ policies.
6. AI-Assisted Fare Estimation and Customer Proposal
The system shall provide an estimated trip cost via a TensorFlow Lite-compatible on-device model using available features (initially distance-based), labelled as advisory.
The system shall combine the estimate with the locked truck-type base rate and truck count according to the documented pricing formula (authoritative server bill in integer cents).

The system shall allow the customer to propose an amount within an administrator-configured adjustment band around the estimate (for example ±10% or ±20%); the backend shall validate the range and record estimate, adjustment limit, customer proposal and rate version.
The system shall not treat the submitted proposal as approved until the administrator accepts it.

The prototype may use the most recent 20 completed trips as a limited training/evaluation window; training/retraining and model-version distribution shall be a separate documented process (TFLite inference alone shall not automatically train a model).
7. Admin Approval, Driver Willingness and Assignment
The system shall allow administrators to review route details, truck count/type, AI estimate, customer proposed fare, allowed adjustment band and total bill.
The system shall allow an admin to approve or reject a request; rejection shall require a reason visible to the customer.

The system shall, for approved requests, allow the admin to ask a candidate driver whether they are willing to accept the trip; only after a positive response shall the admin assign the driver and truck.
The system shall not perform automatic driver matching.
The system shall lock the approved fare; changes shall require an explicit amendment or reapproval record; approve/reject/assign/willingness actions shall be audited.
The system shall activate a trip only after request approval and assignment; the driver shall receive pickup, destination, route, customer contact/chat and payment instructions.

The system shall support defined statuses such as Assigned, En Route to Pickup, Arrived at Pickup, In Transit, Arrived at Destination / Delivered, and Completed, validating allowed transitions and recording timestamps.
The system shall treat payment settlement and trip completion as related but separate states; exceptional completion with outstanding payment shall follow an explicit admin-controlled rule.
9. Real-Time GPS Tracking and Offline Maps
The system shall accept driver GPS updates during permitted trip stages through Socket.IO, associate them with the correct trip, and broadcast to authorized customer and admin views.
The system shall store the latest received location and timestamp and show stale status on temporary disconnection.

The driver app shall download supported map tiles for the planned route area before departure and cache route geometry and essential trip details, using a tile provider whose licence permits the intended caching.

The system shall allow GPS to continue locally without internet; remote users shall not receive live updates until connectivity returns; queued updates shall be timestamped so delayed points are not mistaken for the current location.
The system shall authenticate Socket.IO with JWT and authorize rooms (trip:{id}, user:{id}, admin:ops); GPS writes shall stop when the trip is sealed.
The system shall support trip-related customer–driver and driver–admin conversations with text, images, voice notes and preset messages.
The system shall provide live delivery via Socket.IO where connected while persisting message records in the database.
Priority ranks: Highest (MVP / critical path), Medium (important), Low (supporting / polish).
